```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(812)

### censored Poisson example used for the illustrations in Section 1 and
### developed fully in Section 3: m exact observations, ncen observations
### known only to satisfy y < 2
yobs_d <- c(3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 5, 3)
m_d    <- length(yobs_d)
ncen_d <- 12
n_d    <- m_d + ncen_d

lobs  <- function(l) sum(dpois(yobs_d, l, log = TRUE)) + ncen_d * log(ppois(1, l))
lcomp <- function(l, z) -n_d * l + log(l) * (sum(yobs_d) + sum(z)) - sum(lfactorial(yobs_d))
Qfun  <- function(l, lt) lcomp(l, rep(lt / (1 + lt), ncen_d))
lam   <- seq(0.4, 3.2, length.out = 300)
```

## Overview of EM

### Setup and motivation

Let $Y$ denote the observed data and $\theta$ the parameter, with likelihood
$L(\theta) = P(Y \mid \theta)$. In many models this quantity is itself an
integral (or sum) over latent or missing data $Z$:

$$
P(Y \mid \theta) = \int P(Y, Z \mid \theta) \, dZ .
$$

The integral is what makes direct maximization awkward: it destroys the product
structure that would otherwise make the log-likelihood a sum of simple terms.
The EM algorithm avoids it by working with the complete-data likelihood, which
retains that structure, and correcting for the fact that $Z$ is unobserved.

| | Likelihood | Log-likelihood |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Observed | $L_{\text{obs}}(\theta) = P(Y \mid \theta)$ | $\ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta) = \log P(Y \mid \theta)$ |
| Complete | $L_{\text{comp}}(\theta) = P(Y, Z \mid \theta)$ | $\ell_{\text{comp}}(\theta; Y, Z) = \log P(Y, Z \mid \theta)$ |

: Fixes the notation for the observed-data and complete-data likelihoods used throughout the chapter. Observed and complete likelihoods {#tbl-terminology}

### The algorithm

Start from $\hat\theta^{(0)}$. For $t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$:

**E-step.** Replace $\ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta)$ by the expected complete
log-likelihood,

$$
Q\!\left(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right)
= E_{Z \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)}}\!\left[\ell_{\text{comp}}(\theta; Y, Z)\right].
$$

**M-step.** Maximize it,

$$
\hat\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_{\theta} \; Q\!\left(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right).
$$

Iterate until $\hat\theta^{(t)}$ converges.

::: {.callout-warning}
### A common misreading
$Q$ is an *average of* $\ell_{\text{comp}}(\theta; Y, Z)$ over
$P(Z \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)})$. It is **not**
$\ell_{\text{comp}}\!\left(\theta; Y, E(Z \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)})\right)$ —
that is, EM is not "fill in the missing values with their expectations and
maximize". The two coincide only when $\ell_{\text{comp}}$ happens to be linear
in $Z$, which is true in both examples of this chapter and false in general.
:::

### $Q$ as an average of complete log-likelihoods

Fix $\hat\theta^{(t)}$. Each draw $Z^{(s)} \sim P(Z \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)})$
gives one curve $\ell_{\text{comp}}(\theta; Y, Z^{(s)})$, and
$Q(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)})$ is their expectation. The figure uses the
censored Poisson model of @sec-poisson with $\lambda^{(t)} = 1.5$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q-average
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the $Q$ function of the EM algorithm as the expectation of the complete-data log-likelihood over the unobserved data, approximated here by averaging simulated completions.
#|   Ten complete-data log-likelihood curves, their average, and the exact $Q$ function."
lt <- 1.5; S <- 10
Z <- replicate(S, rbinom(ncen_d, 1, lt / (1 + lt)))
curves <- sapply(1:S, function(s) sapply(lam, lcomp, z = Z[, s]))
Qexact <- sapply(lam, Qfun, lt = lt)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(lam, curves, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = "gray60",
        xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "log-likelihood",
        ylim = range(curves) + c(0, 2))
lines(lam, rowMeans(curves), lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
lines(lam, Qexact, lwd = 3, col = "black", lty = 2)
abline(v = lt, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = c(1, 3, 3), lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       col = c("gray60", "firebrick", "black"),
       legend = c(expression(l[comp](theta*";"*Y*","*Z^(s)) ~ "for 10 draws"),
                  "average of the 10 curves",
                  expression(Q(theta*"|"*hat(theta)^(t)) ~ "(exact expectation)")))
```

### Cross-entropy and Kullback-Leibler distance {#sec-cross-entropy}

For distributions $P$ and $q$ of $Z$, the **cross-entropy** of $q$ relative to $P$ is

$$
H(P, q) = -\int P(z) \log q(z) \, dz = -E_P\!\left[\log q(Z)\right],
$$

so $H(P, P)$ is the entropy of $P$, and the Kullback-Leibler distance is

$$
\mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, q)
= \int P(z) \log \frac{P(z)}{q(z)} \, dz
= H(P, q) - H(P, P) .
$$

**Gibbs' inequality.** $\mathrm{KL}(P \| q) \ge 0$, with equality if and only if
$q = P$. Equivalently, $H(P, q) \ge H(P, P)$: the cross-entropy is smallest at
$q = P$. It follows from $\log x \le x - 1$:

$$
\mathrm{KL}(P \| q) = -\int P(z) \log \frac{q(z)}{P(z)} \, dz
\;\ge\; -\int P(z) \left(\frac{q(z)}{P(z)} - 1\right) dz
= -\int \left[q(z) - P(z)\right] dz = 0 .
$$

### The key identity {#sec-key-identity}

For every $z$,
$\log P(Y \mid \theta) = \log P(Y, z \mid \theta) - \log P(z \mid Y, \theta)$,
because $P(Y, z \mid \theta) = P(Y \mid \theta) \, P(z \mid Y, \theta)$.
Averaging both sides over an *arbitrary* distribution $\tilde P$ of $Z$ (the left
side does not depend on $z$, so the average leaves it unchanged) gives, for any
$\tilde P$,

$$
\ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
= \int \tilde P(z) \log P(Y, z \mid \theta) \, dz
+ H\!\left(\tilde P,\, P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)\right) .
$$ {#eq-key-identity}

The first term is the average complete log-likelihood under $\tilde P$ and the
second is a cross-entropy. For a fixed $\tilde P$ the two terms, as functions
of $\theta$, add up to $\ell_{\text{obs}}$; the figure shows one such split.
The identity is used twice below: for the ascending property of EM and for the
alternating-optimization view of EM.

```{r}
#| label: fig-key-identity
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the key identity: the average complete log-likelihood under a fixed distribution of the hidden data differs from the observed log-likelihood by a cross-entropy.
#|   The gap at each $\\theta$ is the cross-entropy $H(\\tilde P, P_Z(\\cdot \\mid Y, \\theta))$, which can have either sign."
local({
par(mar = c(3.5, 1, 1, 1))
th <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 300)
lo <- function(t) 3.2 - 0.045 * (t - 5.2)^2 + 0.5 * sin(t / 2.2)   # observed log-likelihood
av <- function(t) lo(t) - (1.4 - 0.45 * (t - 3))                    # an arbitrary average complete log-likelihood
plot(th, lo(th), type = "n", ylim = c(-1.5, 4.2), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
mtext(expression(theta), side = 1, line = 1.5, cex = 1.3)
lines(th, lo(th), lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
lines(th, av(th), lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
text(0, lo(0) + 0.9, expression(l[obs](theta)), col = "steelblue", adj = 0, cex = 1.3)
text(9.9, av(9.9) + 0.5, expression(integral(tilde(P)(z)*log*P(Y*","*z*"|"*theta)*dz)),
     col = "firebrick", adj = 1, cex = 1.1)
for (t0 in c(3, 7.5)) {
    arrows(t0, av(t0), t0, lo(t0), code = 3, length = 0.08, lwd = 2)
    text(if (t0 == 3) t0 - 0.15 else t0 + 0.15, (av(t0) + lo(t0)) / 2 - if (t0 == 3) 0.4 else 0, expression(H(tilde(P), P[Z](.*"|"*Y*","*theta))), adj = if (t0 == 3) 1 else 0, cex = 1.2)
    segments(t0, -1.5, t0, min(av(t0), lo(t0)), lty = 3, col = "gray50")
}
axis(1, at = c(3, 7.5), labels = c(expression(theta[1]), expression(theta[2])), tick = TRUE)
})
```

### The ascending property {#sec-ascending}

::: {.callout-note}
### Theorem
$\ell_{\text{obs}}\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t+1)}\right) \ \ge\ \ell_{\text{obs}}\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t)}\right)$
at every iteration.
:::

Plug $\tilde P = P(\cdot \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)})$ into @eq-key-identity. The
first term becomes $Q(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)})$:

$$
\ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
= \underbrace{\int P(z \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)}) \log P(Y, z \mid \theta) \, dz}_{Q(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)})}
+ H\!\left(P(\cdot \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)}),\, P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)\right) .
$$

The M-step makes $Q$ larger, and the cross-entropy is smallest at
$\theta = \hat\theta^{(t)}$ (Gibbs' inequality), so it can only grow when
$\theta$ moves. Both terms increase, hence so does $\ell_{\text{obs}}$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ascending
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the ascending property: moving from the current estimate to the next one raises $Q$ and also raises the cross-entropy gap, so the observed log-likelihood rises by at least the gain in $Q$.
#|   The gap between $\\ell_{\\text{obs}}$ and $Q(\\theta \\mid \\hat\\theta^{(t)})$ is the cross-entropy $H$, smallest at $\\hat\\theta^{(t)}$."
local({
par(mar = c(3.5, 1, 0.5, 1))
th <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 300)
t0 <- 3; t1 <- 6                                         # theta^(t), theta^(t+1)
Q  <- function(t) 2.6 - 0.07 * (t - t1)^2                # Q(theta | theta^(t)), maximised at theta^(t+1)
H  <- function(t) 0.8 + 0.04 * (t - t0)^2                # cross-entropy, smallest at theta^(t) (Gibbs)
lo <- function(t) Q(t) + H(t)                            # l_obs
plot(th, lo(th), type = "n", ylim = c(-0.5, 5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
mtext(expression(theta), side = 1, line = 1.8, cex = 1.3)
lines(th, lo(th), lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
lines(th, Q(th),  lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
text(9.9, lo(9.9) + 0.35, expression(l[obs](theta)), col = "steelblue", adj = 1, cex = 1.3)
text(9.9, Q(9.9) - 0.35, expression(Q(theta*"|"*hat(theta)^(t))), col = "firebrick", adj = 1, cex = 1.3)
segments(c(t0, t1), -0.5, c(t0, t1), c(lo(t0), lo(t1)), lty = 3, col = "gray50")
segments(0.1, c(Q(t0), lo(t0)), t1, c(Q(t0), lo(t0)), lty = 3, col = "gray50")
segments(0.1, c(Q(t1), lo(t1)), t1, c(Q(t1), lo(t1)), lty = 3, col = "gray50")
for (x in c(t0, t1)) arrows(x, Q(x), x, lo(x), code = 3, length = 0.07, lwd = 2)
text(t0 + 0.15, (Q(t0) + lo(t0)) / 2, "H", adj = 0, cex = 1.3)
text(t1 + 0.15, (Q(t1) + lo(t1)) / 2, "H (larger)", adj = 0, cex = 1.3)
arrows(0.3, Q(t0), 0.3, Q(t1), length = 0.07, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
text(0.45, (Q(t0) + Q(t1)) / 2, expression(Delta*Q >= 0), adj = 0, col = "firebrick", cex = 1.1)
arrows(0.3, lo(t0), 0.3, lo(t1), length = 0.07, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
text(0.45, (lo(t0) + lo(t1)) / 2, expression(Delta*l[obs] >= 0), adj = 0, col = "steelblue", cex = 1.2)
axis(1, at = c(0, 10), labels = FALSE, lwd.ticks = 0)                       # the theta axis
arrows(9.6, par("usr")[3], 10.1, par("usr")[3], length = 0.1, xpd = NA)
axis(1, at = c(1, t0, t1), labels = c(expression(hat(theta)^(t-1)), expression(hat(theta)^(t)), expression(hat(theta)^(t+1))), tick = TRUE)
mtext(expression(theta), side = 1, line = 1.8, at = 10.1, cex = 1.3)
})
```

**Proof: comparing two successive points.** Write
$\tilde P = P(\cdot \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)})$ and
$P_\theta = P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)$, so $\tilde P = P_{\hat\theta^{(t)}}$.
Subtract the identity at $\theta = \hat\theta^{(t)}$ from the identity at
$\theta = \hat\theta^{(t+1)}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\text{obs}}\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t+1)}\right) - \ell_{\text{obs}}\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t)}\right)
&= \left[Q\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t+1)} \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right) - Q\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t)} \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right)\right]
+ \left[H\!\left(\tilde P, P_{\hat\theta^{(t+1)}}\right) - H\!\left(\tilde P, \tilde P\right)\right] \\
&= \underbrace{\left[Q\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t+1)} \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right) - Q\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t)} \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right)\right]}_{\ge\, 0 \text{ by the M-step}}
+ \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\tilde P \,\|\, P_{\hat\theta^{(t+1)}}\right)}_{\ge\, 0 \text{ by Gibbs' inequality}} \;\ge\; 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

The second line uses $H(\tilde P, P_{\hat\theta^{(t)}}) = H(\tilde P, \tilde P)$ and
$H(P, q) - H(P, P) = \mathrm{KL}(P \| q)$. $\blacksquare$

Note carefully what the theorem does and does not say: the observed likelihood
never decreases, but that guarantees convergence only to a stationary point,
which may be a local maximum or even a saddle point.

### The function $F(\tilde P, \theta)$ {#sec-F}

For any distribution $\tilde P$ of the hidden data $Z$, define

$$
F(\tilde P, \theta)
= \int \tilde P(z) \log P(Y, z \mid \theta) \, dz + H(\tilde P, \tilde P) ,
$$

the average complete log-likelihood plus the entropy
$H(\tilde P, \tilde P) = -\int \tilde P \log \tilde P$ of $\tilde P$. It has a
second expression:

$$
F(\tilde P, \theta)
= \ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta) - \mathrm{KL}\!\left(\tilde P \,\|\, P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)\right) .
$$

**Why they agree.** Rearrange @eq-key-identity by moving the cross-entropy to
the right-hand side and adding $H(\tilde P, \tilde P)$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \tilde P(z) \log P(Y, z \mid \theta) \, dz + H(\tilde P, \tilde P)
&= \ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta) - \left[H\!\left(\tilde P, P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)\right) - H(\tilde P, \tilde P)\right] \\
&= \ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta) - \mathrm{KL}\!\left(\tilde P \,\|\, P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathrm{KL} \ge 0$, $F(\tilde P, \theta) \le \ell_{\text{obs}}(\theta)$ for every
$\tilde P$ and $\theta$, and equality holds exactly when
$\tilde P = P(\cdot \mid Y, \theta)$.

### EM as alternating optimization {#sec-alternating}

Both steps of EM are coordinate ascent on the single function $F$:

- **E-step** maximizes $F$ over $\tilde P$ with $\theta = \hat\theta^{(t)}$
  fixed. Since $\mathrm{KL} \ge 0$ with equality if and only if
  $\tilde P = P(\cdot \mid Y, \hat\theta^{(t)})$, the E-step sets $\tilde P_t$ to
  the conditional distribution of $Z$.
- **M-step** maximizes $F$ over $\theta$ with $\tilde P_t$ fixed. The entropy
  term does not involve $\theta$, so this is
  $\arg\max_\theta Q(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)})$.
- **Tight bound.** After the E-step, $\mathrm{KL} = 0$ at
  $\theta = \hat\theta^{(t)}$, so the lower bound equals the observed
  log-likelihood there:
  $F(\tilde P_t, \hat\theta^{(t)}) = \ell_{\text{obs}}(\hat\theta^{(t)})$.

The figure shows one full cycle. For a fixed $\tilde P_t$, the curve
$F(\tilde P_t, \cdot)$ is a lower bound of $\ell_{\text{obs}}$. The E-step at
$\hat\theta^{(t)}$ replaces the previous distribution by $\tilde P_t$ and lifts
the bound up to $\ell_{\text{obs}}$ at that point (the green arrows; the dotted
gray curve is the bound before such a lift). The M-step then moves along the new
bound to its maximum $\hat\theta^{(t+1)}$. There $\ell_{\text{obs}}$ lies at
least as high as the bound, which lies at least as high as the old value of
$\ell_{\text{obs}}$:

$$
\ell_{\text{obs}}\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t+1)}\right)
\;\ge\; F\!\left(\tilde P_t, \hat\theta^{(t+1)}\right)
\;\ge\; F\!\left(\tilde P_t, \hat\theta^{(t)}\right)
= \ell_{\text{obs}}\!\left(\hat\theta^{(t)}\right).
$$

This is the ascending property again, now as a statement about alternating
maximization of a single objective, which cannot decrease it. The view also
explains the variational methods used when the E-step is intractable: restrict
$\tilde P$ to a manageable family and accept a bound rather than an equality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-em-steps
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates EM as alternating maximization of $F$: the E-step lifts the lower bound until it touches the observed log-likelihood at the current estimate, and the M-step moves to the maximum of that bound.
#|   Solid blue: $\\ell_{\\text{obs}}(\\theta)$. Light-blue dashed: the bounds $F(\\tilde P_t, \\theta)$ and $F(\\tilde P_{t-1}, \\theta)$. Dotted gray: $F$ for another distribution $\\tilde P$."
local({
par(mar = c(3.5, 1, 0.5, 1))
fcol <- "#6CA6E0"                                                  # light blue: the F curves
th <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 300); t0 <- 3
lo <- function(t) 3.5 - 0.15 * (t - 6.5)^2                      # l_obs
B0 <- function(t) lo(t) - 0.2625 * (t - 1)^2              # F(P~_{t-1}, theta): touches l_obs at theta^(t-1), maximised at theta^(t)
B2 <- function(t) lo(t) - 1.2 - 0.2625 * (t - 1.9)^2                       # F(P~, theta) for another P~ close to P~_{t-1}: below l_obs everywhere, below F(P~_{t-1}) at theta^(t-1)
B1 <- function(t) lo(t) - 0.1 * (t - t0)^2                     # F(P~_t, theta): touches l_obs at theta^(t)
t1 <- optimize(B1, c(0, 10), maximum = TRUE)$maximum             # M-step
plot(th, lo(th), type = "n", ylim = c(-5.8, 5.0), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
lines(th, lo(th), lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
lines(th, ifelse(B0(th) > -3.0, B0(th), NA), lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = fcol)
lines(th, ifelse(B2(th) > -3.0, B2(th), NA), lwd = 3, lty = 3, col = "gray45")
lines(th, ifelse(B1(th) > -3.0, B1(th), NA), lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = fcol)
points(1, lo(1), pch = 19, col = fcol, cex = 1.3)
text(0, 4.8, expression(F(tilde(P)[t], theta) == Q(theta*"|"*hat(theta)^(t)) + H(tilde(P)[t], tilde(P)[t])), col = fcol, adj = 0, cex = 1.2)
text(0, 3.85, expression(phantom(F(tilde(P)[t], theta)) == l[obs](theta) - KL(tilde(P)[t]*"||"*P(.*"|"*Y*","*theta))), col = fcol, adj = 0, cex = 1.2)
segments(c(t0, t1), -5.8, c(t0, t1), c(B0(t0), lo(t1)), lty = 3, col = "gray50")
arrows(t0, B0(t0), t0, lo(t0), length = 0.08, lwd = 3, col = "forestgreen")
arrows(1, B2(1), 1, lo(1) - 0.06, length = 0.08, lwd = 3, col = "forestgreen")   # the E-step before: raises F to l_obs at theta^(t-1)
text(t0 + 0.2, 1.05, expression(bold("E-step:")~tilde(P)[t]~"="~P(.*"|"*Y*","*hat(theta)^(t))), adj = 0, col = "forestgreen", cex = 1.0)
text(1.2, B2(1) + 0.3, expression(bold("E-step")), adj = 0, col = "forestgreen", cex = 1.0)
points(t0, lo(t0), pch = 19, col = fcol, cex = 1.3)
arrows(t0 + 0.1, B1(t0) + 0.04, t1, B1(t1), length = 0.08, lwd = 3, col = "darkorange")
text((t0 + t1) / 2 + 0.2, B1((t0 + t1) / 2) - 0.45, expression(bold("M-step")), col = "darkorange", adj = 0, cex = 1.1)
arrows(t1, B1(t1), t1, lo(t1), length = 0.06, lwd = 2, code = 3)
text(t1 + 0.15, (B1(t1) + lo(t1)) / 2 - 0.1, expression(l[obs]~"is even higher"), adj = 0, cex = 1.0)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 3, lty = c(1, 2, 2, 3), cex = 1.0, y.intersp = 1.3,
       col = c("steelblue", fcol, fcol, "gray45"),
       legend = c(expression(l[obs](theta)),
                  expression(F(tilde(P)[t], theta)),
                  expression(F(tilde(P)[t-1], theta)),
                  expression(F(tilde(P), theta)~"for another"~tilde(P))))
axis(1, at = c(0, 10), labels = FALSE, lwd.ticks = 0)                       # the theta axis
arrows(9.6, par("usr")[3], 10.1, par("usr")[3], length = 0.1, xpd = NA)
axis(1, at = c(1, t0, t1), labels = c(expression(hat(theta)^(t-1)), expression(hat(theta)^(t)), expression(hat(theta)^(t+1))), tick = TRUE)
mtext(expression(theta), side = 1, line = 1.8, at = 10.1, cex = 1.3)
})
```

## Example 1: Two-Component Normal Mixture {#sec-mixture}

### Model and likelihoods

$$
Z_i \sim \text{Bern}(p), \qquad
Y_i \mid Z_i = 1 \sim N(\mu_1, 1), \qquad
Y_i \mid Z_i = 0 \sim N(\mu_0, 1) .
$$

Observed: $y_1, \ldots, y_n$. Hidden: $z_1, \ldots, z_n$. Parameter
$\theta = (\mu_0, \mu_1, p)$.

**Complete likelihood**

$$
P(y, z \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(y_i \mid z_i, \theta) \, P(z_i \mid \theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^{n} \varphi(y_i \mid \mu_{z_i}, 1) \, p^{z_i} (1-p)^{1-z_i} .
$$

**Observed likelihood**, summing out each $z_i$,

$$
P(y \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\left[\varphi(y_i \mid \mu_1, 1)\, p + \varphi(y_i \mid \mu_0, 1)(1 - p)\right] .
$$

The sum inside the product is what makes direct maximization awkward.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mixture-components
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Introduces the two-component normal mixture model by showing that its density is the weighted sum of the two component densities.
#|   The observed density is a sum of two weighted normal components."
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)); mu0 <- 0; mu1 <- 4; p <- 0.3
curve((1 - p) * dnorm(x, mu0), -3.5, 7.5, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
      ylab = "density", xlab = "y", ylim = c(0, 0.3))
curve(p * dnorm(x, mu1), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
curve((1 - p) * dnorm(x, mu0) + p * dnorm(x, mu1), add = TRUE, lwd = 3)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = c(2, 2, 3),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick", "black"),
       legend = c(expression((1-p)*phi(y*"|"*mu[0])),
                  expression(p*phi(y*"|"*mu[1])),
                  expression(f(y*"|"*theta) == "sum")))
```

The marginal density may be bimodal or unimodal depending on $p$ and
$|\mu_1 - \mu_0|$ — a point worth keeping in mind, since the unimodal case is
where EM struggles most.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mixture-shapes
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Shows that a mixture density can look unimodal or bimodal depending on its parameters, which affects how easily those parameters can be estimated.
#|   Separation and mixing proportion determine whether the mixture is visibly bimodal."
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
mix <- function(x, mu0, mu1, p) (1 - p) * dnorm(x, mu0) + p * dnorm(x, mu1)
for (s in list(c(0, 4, 0.5), c(0, 4, 0.15), c(0, 1.5, 0.5))) {
  curve(mix(x, s[1], s[2], s[3]), -4, 7, lwd = 3, xlab = "y", ylab = "density",
        main = bquote(mu[0] == .(s[1]) ~ "," ~ mu[1] == .(s[2]) ~ "," ~ p == .(s[3])))
  y <- ifelse(rbinom(200, 1, s[3]) == 1, rnorm(200, s[2]), rnorm(200, s[1]))
  rug(y, col = "gray40")
}
```

### Complete log-likelihood

With $\log \varphi(y \mid \mu, 1) = -\tfrac{1}{2}(y - \mu)^2 - \log\sqrt{2\pi}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\text{comp}}(\theta; y, z)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[z_i \log p + (1 - z_i)\log(1-p) - \tfrac{1}{2}(y_i - \mu_{z_i})^2\right] + C \\
&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i\right) \log \frac{p}{1-p} + n \log(1-p) \\
&\quad - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[z_i (y_i - \mu_1)^2 + (1 - z_i)(y_i - \mu_0)^2\right] + C .
\end{aligned}
$$

Two features drive everything that follows. The expression is **linear in each
$z_i$**, so the E-step needs only $E(Z_i \mid y_i, \hat\theta^{(t)})$ rather than
the full conditional distribution. And given $z$, the parameters **separate**:
$p$ is a Bernoulli proportion while $\mu_1$ and $\mu_0$ are group means.

### E-step: soft classification

Given $\hat\theta^{(t)} = (\hat\mu_0^{(t)}, \hat\mu_1^{(t)}, \hat p^{(t)})$,
Bayes' rule gives

$$
\hat p_i^{(t)} \equiv P\!\left(Z_i = 1 \mid y_i, \hat\theta^{(t)}\right)
= \frac{\varphi\!\left(y_i \mid \hat\mu_1^{(t)}, 1\right) \hat p^{(t)}}
       {\varphi\!\left(y_i \mid \hat\mu_0^{(t)}, 1\right)\!\left(1 - \hat p^{(t)}\right)
        + \varphi\!\left(y_i \mid \hat\mu_1^{(t)}, 1\right) \hat p^{(t)}} ,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q\!\left(\theta \mid \hat\theta^{(t)}\right)
&= \left(\sum_i \hat p_i^{(t)}\right) \log \frac{p}{1-p} + n \log(1-p) \\
&\quad - \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \left[\hat p_i^{(t)} (y_i - \mu_1)^2 + \left(1 - \hat p_i^{(t)}\right)(y_i - \mu_0)^2\right] .
\end{aligned}
$$

Computationally, $\hat p_i^{(t)}$ must be formed on the log scale. Writing
$a_i = \log \varphi(y_i \mid \hat\mu_1^{(t)}, 1) + \log \hat p^{(t)}$ and
$b_i = \log \varphi(y_i \mid \hat\mu_0^{(t)}, 1) + \log(1 - \hat p^{(t)})$, we
have $\hat p_i^{(t)} = \exp\{a_i - \operatorname{lse}(a_i, b_i)\}$ where
$\operatorname{lse}$ is the log-sum-exp function of the chapter on computer
arithmetic. Forming the ratio directly underflows as soon as an observation sits
far from both means.

```{r}
#| label: fig-estep
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the E-step of EM for a mixture: the responsibility of a component is the posterior probability that an observation came from it.
#|   Left: the responsibility at each $y_i$ is the red share of the total height. Right: responsibility as a function of $y$."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)); mu0 <- 0; mu1 <- 4; p <- 0.3
f0 <- function(x) (1 - p) * dnorm(x, mu0)
f1 <- function(x) p * dnorm(x, mu1)
curve(f0, -3.5, 7.5, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue", ylab = "weighted density",
      xlab = "y", ylim = c(0, 0.3))
curve(f1, add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
yi <- c(-0.5, 1.8, 3.2)
for (y in yi) {
  segments(y, 0, y, f0(y), col = "steelblue", lwd = 4)
  segments(y, f0(y), y, f0(y) + f1(y), col = "firebrick", lwd = 4)
  text(y, f0(y) + f1(y), sprintf("%.2f", f1(y) / (f0(y) + f1(y))), pos = 3, cex = 0.9)
}
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),
       legend = c(expression((1-hat(p))*phi(y*"|"*hat(mu)[0])),
                  expression(hat(p)*phi(y*"|"*hat(mu)[1]))))
curve(f1(x) / (f0(x) + f1(x)), -3.5, 7.5, lwd = 3, xlab = "y",
      ylab = expression(P(Z[i] == 1*"|"*y[i]*","*hat(theta)^(t))))
abline(h = c(0, 1), lty = 3); points(yi, f1(yi) / (f0(yi) + f1(yi)), pch = 19)
```

### M-step: weighted proportions and means

$Q$ separates into one term in $p$ and two in $\mu_1$, $\mu_0$, each maximized
in closed form.

| Update | Stationary equation $\Longrightarrow$ solution |
|:---|:---|
| $p$ | $\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial p} = \dfrac{\sum_i \hat p_i^{(t)}}{p(1-p)} - \dfrac{n}{1-p} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \hat p^{(t+1)} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat p_i^{(t)}$ |
| $\mu_1$ | $\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial \mu_1} = \sum_i \hat p_i^{(t)}(y_i - \mu_1) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \hat\mu_1^{(t+1)} = \dfrac{\sum_i \hat p_i^{(t)} y_i}{\sum_i \hat p_i^{(t)}}$ |
| $\mu_0$ | weights $1 - \hat p_i^{(t)}$: $\;\hat\mu_0^{(t+1)} = \dfrac{\sum_i \left(1 - \hat p_i^{(t)}\right) y_i}{\sum_i \left(1 - \hat p_i^{(t)}\right)}$ |

: Derives the M-step updates for the mixture model, showing that each is a weighted version of the complete-data MLE. M-step updates for the two-component mixture {#tbl-mstep-mixture}

In words: the M-step is the complete-data MLE with each observation split
between the two groups in proportion to its soft classification. Return to the
E-step with $\hat\theta^{(t+1)}$ and recompute the responsibilities.

### Implementation

```{r}
#| label: mix-functions

log_sum_exp <- function(log_x) {
    max_log_x <- max(log_x)
    max_log_x + log(sum(exp(log_x - max_log_x)))
}

### observed log-likelihood, theta = (p, mu1, mu0)
log_like_obs <- function(theta, Y) {
    log_joint <- cbind(log(theta[1])     + dnorm(Y, theta[2], 1, log = TRUE),
                       log(1 - theta[1]) + dnorm(Y, theta[3], 1, log = TRUE))
    sum(apply(log_joint, 1, log_sum_exp))
}

### E-step: responsibilities P(Z_i = 1 | y_i, theta)
e_step <- function(theta, Y) {
    l1 <- dnorm(Y, theta[2], 1, log = TRUE) + log(theta[1])
    l0 <- dnorm(Y, theta[3], 1, log = TRUE) + log(1 - theta[1])
    exp(l1 - apply(cbind(l1, l0), 1, log_sum_exp))
}

### M-step: closed-form weighted updates
m_step <- function(w, Y) {
    c(mean(w),
      sum(Y * w) / sum(w),
      sum(Y * (1 - w)) / sum(1 - w))
}

em_mixnorm <- function(theta0, Y, no_iters) {
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, no_iters + 1, 4,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, c("p", "mu1", "mu0", "log_lik")))
    theta <- theta0
    out[1, ] <- c(theta, log_like_obs(theta, Y))
    for (i in seq_len(no_iters)) {
        theta <- m_step(e_step(theta, Y), Y)
        out[i + 1, ] <- c(theta, log_like_obs(theta, Y))
    }
    out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mix-data
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Shows the simulated data used to demonstrate EM for a mixture; the colours reveal the component labels, which are unobserved in practice and must be inferred.
#|   Simulated mixture data, coloured by the (normally unobserved) component label."

gen_mixnorm <- function(theta, n) {
    Z <- rbinom(n, 1, theta[1])
    Y <- rnorm(n, mean = ifelse(Z == 1, theta[2], theta[3]), sd = 1)
    plot(Y, Z, col = cm.colors(2)[Z + 1], pch = 19,
         ylab = "component label Z")
    Y
}

set.seed(812)
data <- gen_mixnorm(c(0.3, 0, 3), 200)
```

A well-chosen start converges quickly:

```{r}
#| label: mix-run-good
round(em_mixnorm(c(0.5, 0, 3), data, 10), 4)
```

The monotone increase of the last column is the ascending property in action;
it is the single most useful diagnostic when debugging an EM implementation,
since any decrease indicates an error in the E- or M-step.

### Shinylive App for the EM Algorithm for a Normal Mixture {#sec-mixture-app}

There is a [shinylive app](../../shinylive_apps/app_mixture.html) to let you watch the EM algorithm fit a two-component normal mixture, showing how the estimates and the likelihood evolve from iteration to iteration.

### Comparison with general-purpose optimizers

EM is not the only way to maximize the observed likelihood. Applying a
general-purpose optimizer directly requires attention to the parameter space:
$p$ must lie in $(0,1)$, so we reparameterize with the logit.

```{r}
#| label: mix-compare
#| warning: false

neg_loglike_obs <- function(theta, Y) -log_like_obs(theta, Y)

### transformed parameterization: ttheta[1] = logit(p)
neg_loglike_obs_transf <- function(ttheta, Y) {
    theta <- ttheta
    theta[1] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-ttheta[1]))
    neg_loglike_obs(theta, Y)
}

lp0 <- log(0.3 / 0.7)

### Newton-type, untransformed: p can leave (0, 1)
try(nlm(neg_loglike_obs, p = c(0.3, 0, 3), Y = data)$estimate)
try(nlm(neg_loglike_obs, p = c(0.5, -10, 5), Y = data)$estimate)

### Newton-type, transformed
try(nlm(neg_loglike_obs_transf, p = c(lp0, 0, 3), Y = data)$estimate)
try(nlm(neg_loglike_obs_transf, p = c(0, -10, 5), Y = data)$estimate)

### Nelder-Mead
try(optim(c(lp0, 0, 3), neg_loglike_obs_transf, Y = data, method = "Nelder-Mead")$par)
try(optim(c(0, -10, 5), neg_loglike_obs_transf, Y = data, method = "Nelder-Mead")$par)

### Conjugate gradient
try(optim(c(0, 0, 3), neg_loglike_obs_transf, Y = data, method = "CG")$par)
try(optim(c(0, -10, 5), neg_loglike_obs_transf, Y = data, method = "CG")$par)
```

Applied to the observed log-likelihood, these algorithms are more fragile than
EM when the initial values are poorly chosen: the untransformed runs can step
outside $p \in (0,1)$ and produce `NaN`, and the gradient-based methods can stall
in the flat region that a distant start creates. Nelder–Mead is the most stable
of the three here, at the cost of many more function evaluations.

| | EM | General optimizer on $\ell_{\text{obs}}$ |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Constraints | Respected automatically by the M-step | Require reparameterization |
| Monotonicity | Guaranteed; a decrease signals a coding error | None; a bad step can be accepted |
| Derivatives | None needed | Gradient helpful, Hessian better |
| Convergence rate | Linear, rate set by the missing information | Superlinear or quadratic near the optimum |
| Standard errors | Not produced; need Louis' method or a bootstrap | Hessian available directly |
| Behaviour from poor starts | Slow but stable | Can fail outright |

: Helps decide between EM and a general-purpose optimizer by listing the strengths and weaknesses of each. EM compared with direct numerical maximization {#tbl-em-vs-optim}

The last row is the practical trade. EM rarely fails and rarely needs tuning,
which is why it dominates in mixture and latent-variable modelling; it is also
slow near the optimum and gives no standard errors, which is why a hybrid — EM
to get close, then a Newton step to polish and to obtain the Hessian — is common
in production code.

## Example 2: Censored Poisson Data {#sec-poisson}

### Truncated distributions in brief

Let $X \sim f(x)$ and $Y = I(X > c)$. Then $Y \sim \text{Bern}\{P(X > c)\}$, and
the conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ is $f$ restricted to one side of
$c$ and renormalized:

$$
f(x \mid Y = 1) = \frac{f(x)\, I(x > c)}{\int_c^{\infty} f(t)\,dt},
\qquad
f(x \mid Y = 0) = \frac{f(x)\, I(x \le c)}{\int_{-\infty}^{c} f(t)\,dt} .
$$

For discrete $X$ the integrals are sums. This is exactly the distribution the
E-step needs when an observation is known only to lie on one side of $c$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-truncation
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the conditional distributions needed in the E-step when an observation is only known to lie on one side of a cut point.
#|   A density split at a cut point, and the two renormalized conditional densities."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)); cc <- 1
curve(dnorm, -3.5, 3.5, lwd = 3, xlab = "x", ylab = "density",
      main = "f(x) with cut point c")
xs <- seq(cc, 3.5, length.out = 100)
polygon(c(xs, rev(xs)), c(dnorm(xs), rep(0, 100)),
        col = adjustcolor("firebrick", 0.3), border = NA)
xs <- seq(-3.5, cc, length.out = 100)
polygon(c(xs, rev(xs)), c(dnorm(xs), rep(0, 100)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), border = NA)
abline(v = cc, lty = 2); text(cc, 0.38, "c", pos = 4)
text(1.8, 0.05, "P(X > c)", col = "firebrick")
text(-1, 0.1, expression(P(X <= c)), col = "steelblue")
curve(dnorm(x) * (x > cc) / pnorm(cc, lower.tail = FALSE), -3.5, 3.5, lwd = 3,
      col = "firebrick", n = 1001, xlab = "x", ylab = "density",
      main = "conditional densities", ylim = c(0, 1.6))
curve(dnorm(x) * (x <= cc) / pnorm(cc), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue", n = 1001)
abline(v = cc, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("f(x | Y = 0)", "f(x | Y = 1)"))
```

### Data and likelihoods

Let $y_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Pois}(\lambda)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$. The
first $m$ values are observed exactly; for $i > m$ we know only that $y_i < 2$,
recorded as $x_i = I(y_i < 2) = 1$.

**Observed data**: $y_1, \ldots, y_m$ together with
$x_{m+1} = \cdots = x_n = 1$. **Missing**: $y_{m+1}, \ldots, y_n$.

**Complete likelihood**

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{n} f^{\text{Pois}}(y_i \mid \lambda) \cdot \prod_{i=m+1}^{n} I(y_i < 2) .
$$

**Observed likelihood**

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{m} f^{\text{Pois}}(y_i \mid \lambda) \cdot \prod_{i=m+1}^{n} P(y_i < 2 \mid \lambda),
\qquad P(y_i < 2 \mid \lambda) = e^{-\lambda}(1 + \lambda) .
$$

Taking logarithms and dropping constants,

$$
\ell_{\text{obs}}(\lambda) = m \bar y_{1:m} \log \lambda - n \lambda + (n - m)\log(1 + \lambda) .
$$

The second factor makes the MLE nonlinear in $\lambda$; EM sidesteps it.

### E-step

$$
\ell_{\text{comp}}(\lambda) = -n\lambda + (\log \lambda) \sum_{i=1}^{m} y_i
+ (\log \lambda) \underbrace{\sum_{i=m+1}^{n} y_i}_{\text{missing}}
- \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log(y_i!) .
$$

For $i > m$ we have $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, and the Poisson pmf truncated to that set
given $\lambda^{(t)}$ is

$$
P\!\left(y_i = 0 \mid x_i = 1\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \lambda^{(t)}},
\qquad
P\!\left(y_i = 1 \mid x_i = 1\right) = \frac{\lambda^{(t)}}{1 + \lambda^{(t)}} ,
$$

so that

$$
\hat y^{(t)} \equiv E\!\left(y_i \mid x_i = 1, \lambda^{(t)}\right) = \frac{\lambda^{(t)}}{1 + \lambda^{(t)}} .
$$

Since $y_i! = 1$ for $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, the $\log(y_i!)$ term is a known
constant and no further expectation is needed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-poisson-estep
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the E-step for censored Poisson counts: the missing count follows the Poisson distribution restricted to the values consistent with the censoring information.
#|   The conditional distribution of a censored count is the Poisson pmf restricted to $\\{0,1\\}$ and renormalized."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)); lt <- 1.5; k <- 0:6
barplot(dpois(k, lt), names.arg = k,
        col = c("firebrick", "firebrick", rep("gray80", 5)),
        xlab = "y", ylab = "probability",
        main = bquote("Pois(" * lambda^(t) == .(lt) * ")"))
barplot(c(1, lt) / (1 + lt), names.arg = 0:1, col = "firebrick",
        xlab = "y", ylab = "probability",
        main = expression("truncated to {0, 1}: " * P(y[i]*"|"*x[i] == 1)))
```

### M-step and the EM update

$$
Q\!\left(\lambda \mid \lambda^{(t)}\right)
= -n\lambda + (\log \lambda)\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} y_i + (n - m)\,\hat y^{(t)}\right] + C^{(t)} ,
$$

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial \lambda}
= -n + \frac{1}{\lambda}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} y_i + (n - m)\,\hat y^{(t)}\right] = 0 ,
$$

$$
\Longrightarrow \quad
\lambda^{(t+1)} = \frac{m\, \bar y_{1:m} + (n - m)\dfrac{\lambda^{(t)}}{1 + \lambda^{(t)}}}{n} .
$$

The update is the ordinary Poisson MLE — the sample mean — with each censored
value replaced by its conditional expectation. As warned in the overview, this
works *only* because $\ell_{\text{comp}}$ is linear in the missing $y_i$.

### Implementation

```{r}
#| label: poisson-em

### observed log-likelihood, up to an additive constant
##   m    : number of exactly observed counts
##   ybar : their mean
##   ncen : number of counts known only to be < 2
loglik_obs_pois <- function(m, ybar, ncen, lambda) {
    m * ybar * log(lambda) - (m + ncen) * lambda + ncen * log(1 + lambda)
}

em_censored_poisson <- function(m, ybar, ncen,
                                lambda0 = (m * ybar + ncen) / (m + ncen),
                                iterations = 20) {
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iterations + 1, 2,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, c("lambda", "log_lik")))
    lambda <- lambda0
    out[1, ] <- c(lambda, loglik_obs_pois(m, ybar, ncen, lambda))
    for (i in seq_len(iterations)) {
        y_mis  <- lambda / (1 + lambda)                       # E-step
        lambda <- (m * ybar + ncen * y_mis) / (m + ncen)       # M-step
        out[i + 1, ] <- c(lambda, loglik_obs_pois(m, ybar, ncen, lambda))
    }
    out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: poisson-data
set.seed(812)
y    <- rpois(200, 3)
ncen <- sum(y < 2)
m    <- length(y) - ncen
ybar <- mean(y[y >= 2])
c(m = m, ncen = ncen, ybar_observed = ybar)
```

Discarding the censored observations and averaging the rest gives an estimate
clearly above the true mean of $3$: conditioning on $y \ge 2$ removes the small
counts and biases the mean upward. EM recovers them.

```{r}
#| label: poisson-run
round(em_censored_poisson(m, ybar, ncen, lambda0 = 100, iterations = 10), 5)
round(em_censored_poisson(m, ybar, ncen, lambda0 = ybar, iterations = 10), 5)
```

Both starting values reach the same limit, and the log-likelihood increases
monotonically from each. Note how slowly the run from $\lambda^{(0)} = 100$
descends at first — a single-parameter illustration of the same slow-drift
behaviour seen in the mixture app.

### Tangent lower bounds

The bound picture of the overview, for this model. Here $\tilde P_t$ is the
conditional distribution of the $n - m$ censored counts, independent Bernoulli
variables with success probability $p_t = \lambda^{(t)}/(1 + \lambda^{(t)})$, so
its entropy is
$H(\tilde P_t, \tilde P_t) = -(n - m)\left[p_t \log p_t + (1 - p_t)\log(1 - p_t)\right]$.
Each bound

$$
F(\tilde P_t, \lambda)
= Q\!\left(\lambda \mid \lambda^{(t)}\right) + H(\tilde P_t, \tilde P_t)
$$

is the curve $Q(\cdot \mid \lambda^{(t)})$ shifted vertically by this number,
which differs from one iteration to the next but not with $\lambda$. It lies
below $\ell_{\text{obs}}$ and touches it at $\lambda^{(t)}$; maximizing it moves
uphill on $\ell_{\text{obs}}$ itself.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tangent-bound
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates why EM increases the likelihood: each iteration maximizes a lower bound, the Q function plus the entropy of the current conditional distribution, that touches the observed log-likelihood at the current estimate.
#|   Three EM iterations viewed as successive tangent lower bounds of the observed log-likelihood."
lo <- sapply(lam, lobs); top <- max(lo)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(lam, lo, type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = expression(theta),
     ylab = "log-likelihood", ylim = c(top - 16, top + 2.5))
lt <- 0.5; cols <- c("firebrick", "darkorange", "forestgreen")
for (k in 1:3) {
  p_t <- lt / (1 + lt)
  H_t <- -ncen_d * (p_t * log(p_t) + (1 - p_t) * log(1 - p_t))   # H(P_t, P_t)
  lines(lam, sapply(lam, Qfun, lt = lt) + H_t, col = cols[k], lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  points(lt, lobs(lt), pch = 19, col = cols[k])               # = Q(lt | lt) + H_t
  lt_new <- (sum(yobs_d) + ncen_d * lt / (1 + lt)) / n_d     # M-step
  segments(lt_new, top - 16, lt_new, lobs(lt_new), col = cols[k], lty = 3)
  text(lt, lobs(lt), bquote(hat(theta)^(.(k - 1))), pos = 3, col = cols[k], xpd = NA)
  lt <- lt_new
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = c(3, 2), lty = c(1, 2),
       legend = c(expression(l[obs](theta)),
                  expression(F(tilde(P)[t], theta))))
```

### Comparison with general-purpose optimizers

```{r}
#| label: poisson-compare
#| warning: false
neg_loglik_pois <- function(lambda, m, ybar, ncen) {
    -loglik_obs_pois(m, ybar, ncen, lambda)
}

try(nlm(neg_loglik_pois, p = ybar, m = m, ybar = ybar, ncen = ncen)$estimate)
try(nlm(neg_loglik_pois, p = 100,  m = m, ybar = ybar, ncen = ncen)$estimate)
try(optim(ybar, neg_loglik_pois, method = "CG",
          m = m, ybar = ybar, ncen = ncen)$par)
try(optim(100,  neg_loglik_pois, method = "CG",
          m = m, ybar = ybar, ncen = ncen)$par)
```

With one parameter and a smooth concave objective this is an easy problem for
any method; the contrast with the mixture example is instructive, since there
the multimodality and the constraint on $p$ were what made the general
optimizers fragile.

## Example 3: Right-Censored Weibull Data {#sec-weibull}

Survival and reliability data are the standard home of censoring. A unit is
followed until it fails or until the study ends, whichever comes first, and a
unit still running at the end tells us only that its lifetime exceeds the
follow-up time. The Poisson example of @sec-poisson censored a count; here the
missing quantity is a continuous lifetime, and, unlike the Poisson case, the
complete-data log-likelihood is *not* linear in it.

### Data and likelihoods

Let $T_1, \ldots, T_n$ be independent lifetimes with the Weibull density and
survival function

$$
f(t \mid k, \lambda) = \frac{k}{\lambda}\Big(\frac{t}{\lambda}\Big)^{k-1} e^{-(t/\lambda)^k},
\qquad
S(t \mid k, \lambda) = P(T > t) = e^{-(t/\lambda)^k},
\qquad t > 0,
$$

with shape $k > 0$ and scale $\lambda > 0$ ($k = 1$ is the exponential
distribution); @fig-weibull-densities shows how they change the density. Unit $i$ is followed up to a censoring time $c_i$, independent
of $T_i$, and we record

$$
y_i = \min(T_i, c_i), \qquad \delta_i = I(T_i \le c_i) .
$$

Let $d = \sum_i \delta_i$ be the number of observed failures. For a censored
unit ($\delta_i = 0$) we know only that $T_i > c_i = y_i$.

**Observed data**: $(y_i, \delta_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$. **Missing**: $T_i$ for
the units with $\delta_i = 0$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-weibull-densities
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates how the shape $k$ and the scale $\\lambda$ change the Weibull density.
#|   Left: different shapes with $\\lambda = 10$ ($k < 1$ is decreasing with a spike at 0, $k = 1$ is exponential, $k > 1$ has a mode). Right: different scales with $k = 2$, which stretch the density along the time axis."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
tt <- seq(0.01, 30, length.out = 400)
ks <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 3); cl <- c("firebrick", "darkorange", "steelblue", "darkgreen")
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 30), ylim = c(0, 0.3), xlab = "t", ylab = "density",
     main = expression("shape varies, " * lambda == 10))
for (j in seq_along(ks)) lines(tt, dweibull(tt, ks[j], 10), col = cl[j], lwd = 2)
legend("topright", paste0("k = ", ks), col = cl, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
ls_ <- c(5, 10, 20)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, 0.23), xlab = "t", ylab = "density",
     main = expression("scale varies, " * k == 2))
tt2 <- seq(0.01, 40, length.out = 400)
for (j in seq_along(ls_)) lines(tt2, dweibull(tt2, 2, ls_[j]), col = cl[j], lwd = 2)
legend("topright", paste0("lambda = ", ls_), col = cl, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

**Observed likelihood.** A failure contributes its density, a censored unit its
survival probability:

$$
L_{\text{obs}}(k, \lambda) = \prod_{i:\,\delta_i = 1} f(y_i \mid k, \lambda)
\prod_{i:\,\delta_i = 0} S(y_i \mid k, \lambda),
$$

$$
\ell_{\text{obs}}(k, \lambda)
= d \log k - d\, k \log \lambda + (k - 1) \sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 1} \log y_i
- \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big(\frac{y_i}{\lambda}\Big)^k .
$$

If $k$ is known, setting $\partial \ell_{\text{obs}} / \partial \lambda = 0$
gives $\hat\lambda^k = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^k / d$, but for unknown $k$ there is no
closed form, and the maximization has to be done numerically. EM replaces it by
a sequence of simpler problems.

**Complete-data log-likelihood.** If all $T_i$ were seen,

$$
\ell_{\text{comp}}(k, \lambda)
= n \log k - n k \log \lambda + (k - 1) \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log T_i
- \lambda^{-k} \sum_{i=1}^{n} T_i^{\,k} .
$$

It depends on the missing $T_i$ through $\log T_i$ and $T_i^{\,k}$, two
*nonlinear* functions. As warned in the overview, the E-step therefore needs
$E(\log T_i \mid \cdot)$ and $E(T_i^{\,k} \mid \cdot)$, not
$\big(\log E(T_i \mid \cdot)\big)$ or $E(T_i \mid \cdot)^k$, and substituting
$E(T_i \mid \cdot)$ for $T_i$ would give the wrong algorithm.

### E-step

Write $\theta^{(t)} = (k_t, \lambda_t)$ for the current value. The key fact is
that $U = (T/\lambda_t)^{k_t}$ has the standard exponential distribution, so
for a censored unit

$$
T_i > c_i \iff U_i > a_i, \qquad a_i = (c_i / \lambda_t)^{k_t},
$$

and by the memoryless property of the exponential distribution
$U_i \mid U_i > a_i \;\overset{d}{=}\; a_i + E$ with $E \sim \text{Exp}(1)$. Hence,
given the data and $\theta^{(t)}$,

$$
T_i = \lambda_t \,(a_i + E)^{1/k_t}, \qquad E \sim \text{Exp}(1),
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-weibull-estep
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the conditional distribution of a censored lifetime in the E-step.
#|   Left: the Weibull density $f(t \\mid k_t, \\lambda_t)$ and, in red, the density of $T$ given $T > c$, which is the part of $f$ beyond $c$ divided by $S(c)$. Right: the same on the exponential scale $U = (T/\\lambda_t)^{k_t}$, where the conditional density $e^{-(u - a)}$ is the standard exponential shifted to start at $a = (c/\\lambda_t)^{k_t}$ (the memoryless property)."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
k_t <- 1.5; lam_t <- 10; cc <- 12; a_c <- (cc / lam_t)^k_t
tt <- seq(0, 30, length.out = 500)
plot(tt, dweibull(tt, k_t, lam_t), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "t", ylab = "density",
     ylim = c(0, 0.2), main = expression("Weibull: " * f(t) * " and " * f(t * "|" * T > c)))
tb <- tt[tt >= cc]
polygon(c(cc, tb, 30), c(0, dweibull(tb, k_t, lam_t), 0), col = adjustcolor("gray70", 0.6), border = NA)
lines(tb, dweibull(tb, k_t, lam_t) / pweibull(cc, k_t, lam_t, lower.tail = FALSE),
      col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(v = cc, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("f(t)", "f(t) beyond c (area S(c))", "f(t | T > c)"),
       col = c("black", "gray70", "firebrick"), lwd = c(2, 8, 2), bty = "n")
uu <- seq(0, 6, length.out = 500)
plot(uu, dexp(uu), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "u", ylab = "density", ylim = c(0, 1.5),
     main = expression("exponential scale: " * U == (T / lambda[t])^{k[t]}))
ub <- uu[uu >= a_c]
polygon(c(a_c, ub, 6), c(0, dexp(ub), 0), col = adjustcolor("gray70", 0.6), border = NA)
lines(ub, dexp(ub - a_c), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(v = a_c, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Exp(1)", "Exp(1) beyond a (area e^-a)", "u | U > a: a + Exp(1)"),
       col = c("black", "gray70", "firebrick"), lwd = c(2, 8, 2), bty = "n")
```

@fig-weibull-estep illustrates the two conditional distributions. which gives both expectations that are needed. For any power $s > 0$,

$$
E\big(T_i^{\,s} \mid T_i > c_i, \theta^{(t)}\big)
= \lambda_t^{\,s}\, E\big[(a_i + E)^{s/k_t}\big]
= \lambda_t^{\,s}\, e^{a_i}\, \Gamma\!\big(1 + s/k_t,\; a_i\big),
$$

where $\Gamma(b, a) = \int_a^\infty u^{b-1} e^{-u}\,du$ is the upper incomplete gamma
function. For the power $s = k_t$ this reduces to the elementary expression
$\lambda_t^{k_t}(a_i + 1) = c_i^{k_t} + \lambda_t^{k_t}$: a censored unit is
expected to run on for one more unit of the exponential clock. For the
logarithm, integration by parts gives

$$
E\big(\log T_i \mid T_i > c_i, \theta^{(t)}\big)
= \log \lambda_t + \frac{1}{k_t}\Big[\log a_i + e^{a_i} E_1(a_i)\Big],
\qquad E_1(a) = \int_a^\infty \frac{e^{-u}}{u}\,du ,
$$

the exponential integral. For an observed failure the expectations are simply
$y_i^{\,s}$ and $\log y_i$. Collect

$$
S_{\log}^{(t)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} E\big(\log T_i \mid \cdot\big),
\qquad
S_k^{(t)}(k) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} E\big(T_i^{\,k} \mid \cdot\big)
= \sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 1} y_i^{\,k}
+ \sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 0} \lambda_t^{\,k}\, e^{a_i}\, \Gamma\!\big(1 + k/k_t,\; a_i\big) .
$$

Then

$$
Q\big(k, \lambda \mid \theta^{(t)}\big)
= n \log k - n k \log \lambda + (k - 1)\, S_{\log}^{(t)} - \lambda^{-k} S_k^{(t)}(k) .
$$

### M-step

For fixed $k$, $\partial Q / \partial \lambda = -nk/\lambda + k \lambda^{-k-1} S_k^{(t)}(k) = 0$ gives

$$
\lambda^{k} = \frac{1}{n} S_k^{(t)}(k) ,
$$

the Weibull MLE of $\lambda^k$ for complete data, with each $T_i^{\,k}$ replaced by
its conditional expectation. Substituting this back gives the profile of $Q$ in
$k$ alone, up to a constant,

$$
Q_p(k) = n \log k - n \log\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{n} S_k^{(t)}(k)\Big) + (k - 1)\, S_{\log}^{(t)},
$$

so the M-step maximizes the one-dimensional function $Q_p$ (here by `optimize`)
and then sets $\lambda_{t+1} = \big(S_k^{(t)}(k_{t+1})/n\big)^{1/k_{t+1}}$.
Because $S_k^{(t)}(k)$ depends on $k$, no closed form exists for $k_{t+1}$, but
every M-step is a cheap one-dimensional problem, whereas the original problem
couples $k$ and $\lambda$ through the censored terms.

### Special case: known shape

If $k$ is known, only $E(T_i^{\,k} \mid \cdot) = c_i^{\,k} + \lambda_t^{\,k}$ is
needed, and the update is in closed form,

$$
\lambda_{t+1}^{\,k}
= \frac{1}{n}\Big[\sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 1} y_i^{\,k}
+ \sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 0} \big(y_i^{\,k} + \lambda_t^{\,k}\big)\Big]
= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^{\,k} + (n - d)\,\lambda_t^{\,k}}{n} ,
$$

the same structure as the Poisson update: the complete-data estimate with each
censored value replaced by its conditional expectation. Its fixed point
satisfies $\lambda^k = \big(\sum_i y_i^{\,k} + (n-d)\lambda^k\big)/n$, that is
$\lambda^k = \sum_i y_i^{\,k}/d$, which is the MLE. Subtracting the fixed point
from the update gives, exactly,

$$
\lambda_{t+1}^{\,k} - \hat\lambda^{\,k} = \frac{n - d}{n}\,\big(\lambda_t^{\,k} - \hat\lambda^{\,k}\big) ,
$$

so the error contracts by the *fraction of censored units* at every iteration.
This is the general rule that EM converges at a rate equal to the fraction of
missing information: with 10% censoring the algorithm is fast, and with 70%
censoring it is slow.

### Implementation

```{r}
#| label: weibull-em

### observed log-likelihood; y = min(T, c), event = (T <= c)
loglik_weib <- function(k, lam, y, event) {
    sum(event * (log(k) - k * log(lam) + (k - 1) * log(y))) - sum((y / lam)^k)
}

### E(log(a + E)), E ~ Exp(1): the integral behind E(log T | T > c)
elog_term <- function(a) integrate(function(x) log(a + x) * exp(-x), 0, Inf)$value

### E-step: the two sums S_log and S_k(.) of the text
e_step_weib <- function(y, event, k_t, lam_t) {
    cen <- !event
    a   <- (y[cen] / lam_t)^k_t
    elogT <- log(y)
    elogT[cen] <- log(lam_t) + vapply(a, elog_term, numeric(1)) / k_t
    ## S_k(k) = sum_i E(T_i^k | data, theta_t); computed on the log scale so that
    ## a large a = (c / lam_t)^k_t cannot overflow exp(a)
    S_k <- function(k) {
        s <- k / k_t
        sum(y[event]^k) +
            sum(lam_t^k * exp(a + pgamma(a, s + 1, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) +
                              lgamma(s + 1)))
    }
    list(S_log = sum(elogT), S_k = S_k)
}

### EM: the M-step maximizes the profile Q_p(k) in one dimension, then sets lambda
em_weib <- function(y, event, k0 = 1, lam0 = mean(y), iterations = 200, tol = 1e-10) {
    n <- length(y); k <- k0; lam <- lam0
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iterations + 1, 3,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, c("k", "lambda", "log_lik")))
    out[1, ] <- c(k, lam, loglik_weib(k, lam, y, event))
    for (i in seq_len(iterations)) {
        E  <- e_step_weib(y, event, k, lam)                                  # E-step
        Qp <- function(kk) n * log(kk) - n * log(E$S_k(kk) / n) + (kk - 1) * E$S_log
        k  <- optimize(Qp, c(k / 4, 4 * k), maximum = TRUE, tol = 1e-12)$maximum   # M-step
        lam <- (E$S_k(k) / n)^(1 / k)
        out[i + 1, ] <- c(k, lam, loglik_weib(k, lam, y, event))
        if (abs(out[i + 1, 3] - out[i, 3]) < tol) {
            out <- out[seq_len(i + 1), , drop = FALSE]; break
        }
    }
    out
}

### known shape: the closed-form update of the text
em_weib_known_k <- function(y, event, k, lam0 = mean(y), iterations = 200, tol = 1e-10) {
    n <- length(y); d <- sum(event); path <- lam <- lam0
    for (i in seq_len(iterations)) {
        lam_new <- ((sum(y^k) + (n - d) * lam^k) / n)^(1 / k)
        path <- c(path, lam_new)
        if (abs(lam_new - lam) < tol * lam) break
        lam <- lam_new
    }
    path
}
```

Before using the E-step it is worth checking the two formulas against brute
force. Draw $T = \lambda_t (a + E)^{1/k_t}$ many times and compare:

```{r}
#| label: weibull-check
set.seed(812)
a <- 1.3; k_t <- 1.7; lam_t <- 8
Tsim <- lam_t * (a + rexp(1e6))^(1 / k_t)
c(monte_carlo = mean(log(Tsim)),  formula = log(lam_t) + elog_term(a) / k_t)
c(monte_carlo = mean(Tsim^2),
  formula = lam_t^2 * exp(a + pgamma(a, 2 / k_t + 1, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) +
                          lgamma(2 / k_t + 1)))
```

### Simulation 1: one data set

Lifetimes are Weibull with $k = 1.5$ and $\lambda = 10$, and censoring times are
exponential with mean $20$, independent of the lifetimes, which censors about
30% of $n = 200$ units.

```{r}
#| label: weibull-data
set.seed(812)
n <- 200; k_true <- 1.5; lam_true <- 10
Tlife <- rweibull(n, k_true, lam_true)
cens  <- rexp(n, 1 / 20)
y     <- pmin(Tlife, cens)
event <- Tlife <= cens
c(censored_fraction = mean(!event), failures = sum(event))
```

@fig-weibull-data1 shows the data against the generating density: a censored unit
is plotted at its censoring time, so the red points sit where the follow-up ended
and say only that the lifetime lies to their right.

```{r}
#| label: fig-weibull-data1
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the data of Simulation 1 with the Weibull density that generated the lifetimes.
#|   Black points are observed failures and red points are right-censored times; heights are random and only separate the points."
### the data with the generating density: failures in black, censored times in red
plot_weib_data <- function(y, event, k, lam, main, xmax = max(y)) {
    tt <- seq(0, xmax, length.out = 300); dens <- dweibull(tt, k, lam)
    ytop <- max(dens[is.finite(dens)]) * 1.25
    plot(tt, dens, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, ytop), xlim = c(0, xmax),
         xlab = "time", ylab = "density", main = main)
    h <- runif(length(y), 0, 0.22 * ytop)                  # random heights, to separate the points
    points(y[event],  h[event],  pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6))
    points(y[!event], h[!event], pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = adjustcolor("red", 0.7))
    legend("topright", c("true density", "failure", "censored"), lwd = c(2, NA, NA),
           pch = c(NA, 16, 16), col = c("black", "black", "red"), bty = "n")
}

set.seed(1)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot_weib_data(y, event, k_true, lam_true, "Simulation 1: n = 200", xmax = 30)
```

```{r}
#| label: weibull-run
fit <- em_weib(y, event, k0 = 1, lam0 = mean(y))
round(fit[c(1:6, nrow(fit)), ], 5)
nrow(fit) - 1                                     # iterations used
all(diff(fit[, "log_lik"]) >= -1e-10)             # ascending property
```

The log-likelihood increases at every iteration, as the ascending property
requires. To check the limit, compare with a direct numerical maximization of
$\ell_{\text{obs}}$ and with the Weibull regression of the `survival` package,
which fits the same model by a Newton-type method:

```{r}
#| label: weibull-check-fit
direct <- optim(c(0, 0), function(p) -loglik_weib(exp(p[1]), exp(p[2]), y, event),
                control = list(reltol = 1e-14))
sr <- survival::survreg(survival::Surv(y, event) ~ 1, dist = "weibull")
rbind(EM      = fit[nrow(fit), c("k", "lambda")],
      optim   = exp(direct$par),
      survreg = c(1 / sr$scale, exp(coef(sr))))
```

The three agree to several digits. @fig-weibull-paths shows the EM paths from
three different starting values on the contours of $\ell_{\text{obs}}$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-weibull-paths
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates EM for right-censored Weibull data from three starting values: every run climbs the observed log-likelihood to the same maximum.
#|   Contours of the observed log-likelihood in $(k, \\lambda)$ with the EM paths; the cross marks the true value and the circle the maximum likelihood estimate."
kg <- seq(0.6, 3, length.out = 120); lg <- seq(6, 16, length.out = 120)
ll <- outer(kg, lg, Vectorize(function(k, l) loglik_weib(k, l, y, event)))
contour(kg, lg, ll, levels = max(ll) - c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64),
        labels = paste0("-", c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)), xlab = "shape k",
        ylab = "scale lambda", col = "gray60")
starts <- list(c(0.7, 14), c(2.8, 7), c(2.5, 15))
cols <- c("firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen")
for (j in seq_along(starts)) {
    p <- em_weib(y, event, starts[[j]][1], starts[[j]][2])
    lines(p[, "k"], p[, "lambda"], type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = cols[j])
}
points(k_true, lam_true, pch = 4, lwd = 2, cex = 1.5)
points(fit[nrow(fit), "k"], fit[nrow(fit), "lambda"], pch = 1, cex = 2)
```

### Simulation 2: the censoring rate sets the speed

For known shape ($k = 2$) the contraction factor is the censored fraction, as
derived above. The simulation draws four data sets of $n = 400$ lifetimes with
increasing censoring (@fig-weibull-data2), then runs the closed-form EM on each
and compares the observed ratio of successive errors with the censored fraction
(@tbl-weibull-rate).

```{r}
#| label: fig-weibull-data2
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the four data sets of Simulation 2 ($n = 400$, $k = 2$, $\\lambda = 10$), from light to heavy censoring.
#|   Black points are failures and red points are right-censored times; the curve is the generating density."
set.seed(812)
mean_cens <- c(200, 30, 12, 6)
rate_data <- lapply(mean_cens, function(mc, n = 400, k = 2, lam = 10) {
    Tl <- rweibull(n, k, lam); cc <- rexp(n, 1 / mc)
    list(y = pmin(Tl, cc), event = Tl <= cc)
})
set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (j in 1:4) {
    d <- rate_data[[j]]
    plot_weib_data(d$y, d$event, 2, 10, paste0("censored: ", round(100 * mean(!d$event)), "%"),
                   xmax = 30)
}
```

The *error* of iteration $t$ is the distance to the limit,
$e_t = |\lambda_t - \hat\lambda|$, where $\hat\lambda$ is the value the
iteration converges to (the last iterate of the run, which equals the MLE
$(\sum_i y_i^k / d)^{1/k}$ up to the tolerance). The *error ratio* is
$e_{t+1}/e_t$, the factor by which one more EM iteration shrinks the error; a
ratio of $0.5$ means the error halves each iteration, and a ratio close to $1$
means the iteration crawls. The derivation above shows that
$\lambda^k_{t+1} - \hat\lambda^k = \frac{n-d}{n}(\lambda^k_t - \hat\lambda^k)$ holds
exactly, so the ratio for $\lambda^k$ is the censored fraction at every
iteration; for $\lambda$ itself it approaches the same value once the iterates are
close to $\hat\lambda$. The table reports the ratio of the errors at iterations
$7$ and $6$ (late enough for the approach to the limit, early enough that
rounding error in $\hat\lambda$ does not matter), next to the realized
censored fraction. The number of iterations needed to gain a fixed accuracy is
then about $\log(\text{tolerance}) / \log(\text{ratio})$, which is why the
iteration count grows sharply as the ratio approaches 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-weibull-rate
#| tbl-cap: "Shows that the error ratio of the closed-form EM for known shape is close to the censored fraction, so heavier censoring needs more iterations.
#|   Known-shape EM on the four data sets of Simulation 2: realized censored fraction, iterations to convergence, and the error ratio $e_7/e_6$ of two successive iterations."
rate_row <- function(dat, k = 2) {
    p   <- em_weib_known_k(dat$y, dat$event, k, tol = 1e-13)
    err <- abs(p - tail(p, 1))
    c(censored = mean(!dat$event), iterations = length(p) - 1,
      error_ratio = err[8] / err[7])
}
rate_tab <- t(sapply(rate_data, rate_row))
knitr::kable(round(rate_tab, 3))
```

The same holds for the full two-parameter EM, whose speed also falls as
censoring grows (@tbl-weibull-mc, column *iterations*).

### Simulation 3: what ignoring the censoring costs

Finally, a Monte Carlo experiment with $n = 100$ and true values $k = 2$,
$\lambda = 10$. Each data set is analysed in three ways: EM with the censoring
accounted for, discarding the censored units, and treating the censoring times
as if they were failure times. The averages over 200 replications are in
@tbl-weibull-mc. @fig-weibull-data3 shows one simulated data set at each censoring level.

```{r}
#| label: fig-weibull-data3
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates one simulated data set ($n = 100$, $k = 2$, $\\lambda = 10$) at each of the four censoring levels of Simulation 3.
#|   Black points are failures and red points are right-censored times; the curve is the generating density."
set.seed(3)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (mc in c(200, 30, 12, 6)) {
    Tl <- rweibull(100, 2, 10); cc <- rexp(100, 1 / mc)
    plot_weib_data(pmin(Tl, cc), Tl <= cc, 2, 10,
                   paste0("censored: ", round(100 * mean(Tl > cc)), "%"), xmax = 30)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-weibull-mc
#| tbl-cap: "Shows what ignoring the censoring costs: EM stays near the truth while the two naive analyses are biased.
#|   Monte Carlo averages over 200 data sets of $n = 100$ (true $k = 2$, $\\lambda = 10$), for four censoring levels: the EM estimates are close to the truth at every level, while discarding the censored units or treating them as failures biases the scale (and the shape) downward, increasingly so with the amount of censoring."
set.seed(812)
sim_weib <- function(mean_cens, nrep = 200, n = 100, k = 2, lam = 10) {
    res <- replicate(nrep, {
        Tl <- rweibull(n, k, lam); cc <- rexp(n, 1 / mean_cens)
        yy <- pmin(Tl, cc); ee <- Tl <= cc
        r   <- em_weib(yy, ee, 1, mean(yy), tol = 1e-8)
        drop <- survival::survreg(survival::Surv(yy[ee], rep(TRUE, sum(ee))) ~ 1,
                                  dist = "weibull")
        asfail <- survival::survreg(survival::Surv(yy, rep(TRUE, n)) ~ 1, dist = "weibull")
        c(censored = mean(!ee), iterations = nrow(r) - 1,
          k_EM = unname(r[nrow(r), "k"]), lambda_EM = unname(r[nrow(r), "lambda"]),
          k_drop = 1 / drop$scale, lambda_drop = unname(exp(coef(drop))),
          k_asfail = 1 / asfail$scale, lambda_asfail = unname(exp(coef(asfail))))
    })
    rowMeans(res)
}
mc <- t(sapply(c(200, 30, 12, 6), sim_weib))
mc <- as.data.frame(round(mc, 2))
names(mc) <- c("censored", "iterations", "k_EM", "lam_EM", "k_drop", "lam_drop",
               "k_fail", "lam_fail")
gt::gt(mc) |>
    gt::tab_spanner("EM", columns = c(k_EM, lam_EM)) |>
    gt::tab_spanner("Drop Censored Obs", columns = c(k_drop, lam_drop)) |>
    gt::tab_spanner("As Failures", columns = c(k_fail, lam_fail)) |>
    gt::cols_label(censored = "censored", iterations = "iterations",
                   k_EM = gt::md("*k*"), k_drop = gt::md("*k*"), k_fail = gt::md("*k*"),
                   lam_EM = "λ", lam_drop = "λ",
                   lam_fail = "λ")
```

With light censoring all three analyses are close. As censoring grows,
discarding the censored units removes exactly the long lifetimes and treating
the censoring times as failures declares them to have failed early, so both
underestimate the scale and the shape; the EM estimates stay near the truth
because each censored unit contributes what the model says about its unobserved
lifetime, not a made-up value.

## Example 4: Logistic Regression as a Latent-Variable Problem {#sec-logistic}

Logistic regression is usually fitted directly, by Newton's method on the
observed log-likelihood (`glm` uses iteratively reweighted least squares, which
for the logit link is exactly Newton's method). It can also be viewed as a
missing-data problem: each binary response is a thresholded version of an
unobserved continuous variable. This example derives the EM algorithm implied
by that view and compares it with `glm`. The point is not speed (EM will lose)
but to see the general machinery at work on a familiar model, and to see the
fraction of missing information decide the convergence rate once more.

### The latent-variable model

Let $x_i$ be the covariate vector of unit $i$ (with a leading 1) and
$\mu_i = x_i^\top\beta$. Suppose

$$
z_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Logistic}(0, 1),
\qquad y_i = I(z_i > 0),
$$

where the standard logistic distribution has CDF and density

$$
F(r) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-r}}, \qquad f(r) = F(r)\{1 - F(r)\} = \frac{e^{-r}}{(1 + e^{-r})^2} .
$$

That is, $z_i \sim \text{Logistic}(x_i^\top\beta)$ and only its sign is recorded.
Because the logistic density is symmetric,

$$
P(y_i = 1 \mid \beta) = P(\varepsilon_i > -\mu_i) = 1 - F(-\mu_i) = F(\mu_i)
= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x_i^\top\beta}} ,
$$

which is the logistic regression model. The left panel of @fig-logit-latent
shows $p_i = P(y_i = 1)$ as the area of the latent density to the right of 0.
(With a normal $\varepsilon_i$ the same construction gives probit regression.)

**Observed data**: $(x_i, y_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$. **Missing**: $z_1, \ldots, z_n$.

**Complete log-likelihood.** Since $y_i$ is a function of $z_i$, the complete
data are just the $z_i$, and

$$
\ell_{\text{comp}}(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(z_i - x_i^\top\beta),
\qquad \log f(r) = -r - 2\log(1 + e^{-r}) .
$$

This is a linear regression with logistic instead of normal errors. It is not
linear in $z_i$, so the E-step needs the whole conditional distribution of
$z_i$, not just its mean (the warning of the overview), and the M-step has no
closed form.

**Observed log-likelihood.**

$$
\ell_{\text{obs}}(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \big\{ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \big\},
\qquad p_i = F(x_i^\top\beta) .
$$

### E-step

Given $y_i$ and the current $\beta_t$, $z_i$ has the
$\text{Logistic}(\mu_i^{(t)})$ density truncated to $(0, \infty)$ if $y_i = 1$
and to $(-\infty, 0]$ if $y_i = 0$ (right panel of @fig-logit-latent). The
truncation is easiest to describe on the probability scale. Let
$U_i = F(z_i - \mu_i^{(t)})$. Without conditioning, $U_i$ is uniform on
$(0, 1)$; the event $z_i > 0$ is the event $U_i > F(-\mu_i^{(t)}) = 1 - p_i^{(t)}$.
Hence

$$
U_i \mid y_i, \beta_t \sim
\begin{cases}
\text{Unif}\big(1 - p_i^{(t)},\ 1\big), & y_i = 1, \\
\text{Unif}\big(0,\ 1 - p_i^{(t)}\big), & y_i = 0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
z_i = \mu_i^{(t)} + \operatorname{logit}(U_i) .
$$

Write $(a_i, b_i)$ for the interval of $U_i$. Then

$$
Q(\beta \mid \beta_t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{b_i - a_i}\int_{a_i}^{b_i}
\log f\big(\mu_i^{(t)} + \operatorname{logit}(u) - x_i^\top\beta\big)\, du .
$$

The integrals have no closed form, but each is one-dimensional over a known
interval, so Gauss–Legendre quadrature with $K$ nodes $u_{ik}$ and weights
$w_k$ ($\sum_k w_k = 1$) on $(a_i, b_i)$ handles it:

$$
Q(\beta \mid \beta_t) \approx \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{k=1}^K w_k \log f(z_{ik} - x_i^\top\beta),
\qquad z_{ik} = \mu_i^{(t)} + \operatorname{logit}(u_{ik}) .
$$

The E-step therefore replaces each binary $y_i$ by $K$ weighted pseudo-values
$z_{ik}$ of the latent variable, all on the side of 0 that $y_i$ dictates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-logit-latent
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates logistic regression as a thresholded latent variable and the conditional distributions of the latent variable used in the E-step.
#|   Left: the latent $z_i \\sim \\text{Logistic}(\\mu_i)$ with $\\mu_i = 0.8$; the red area to the right of 0 is $p_i = P(y_i = 1)$ and the grey area is $1 - p_i$. Right: the density of $z_i$ given $y_i = 1$ (red) and given $y_i = 0$ (grey), each the matching part of the left density renormalized."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
mu_i <- 0.8; p_i <- plogis(mu_i); zz <- seq(-6, 7, length.out = 500)
dz <- dlogis(zz, mu_i)
plot(zz, dz, type = "n", xlab = "z", ylab = "density",
     main = bquote(list("Logistic(" * mu[i] == .(mu_i) * ")", p[i] == .(round(p_i, 3)))))
polygon(c(0, zz[zz > 0], max(zz)), c(0, dz[zz > 0], 0), col = "firebrick", border = NA)
polygon(c(min(zz), zz[zz <= 0], 0), c(0, dz[zz <= 0], 0), col = "gray80", border = NA)
lines(zz, dz, lwd = 2); abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
text(2.2, 0.06, "y = 1", col = "white", font = 2); text(-1.6, 0.03, "y = 0", font = 2)
plot(zz, ifelse(zz > 0, dz / p_i, NA), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick",
     ylim = c(0, max(dz / (1 - p_i))), xlab = "z", ylab = "density",
     main = expression("conditional density of " * z[i] * " given " * y[i]))
lines(zz, ifelse(zz <= 0, dz / (1 - p_i), NA), lwd = 2, col = "gray50")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("given y = 1", "given y = 0"), col = c("firebrick", "gray50"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

### M-step

The M-step maximizes the weighted pseudo-data log-likelihood of the
logistic-error regression. With $r_{ik} = z_{ik} - x_i^\top\beta$ and
$\psi(r) = -\frac{d}{dr}\log f(r) = 2F(r) - 1$, so that $\psi'(r) = 2f(r)$,
its gradient and Hessian are

$$
\nabla_\beta Q = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \sum_{k=1}^K w_k\, \psi(r_{ik}),
\qquad
\nabla^2_\beta Q = -\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i^\top \sum_{k=1}^K w_k\, 2 f(r_{ik}) .
$$

The Hessian is negative definite, so $Q(\cdot \mid \beta_t)$ is concave and a
few Newton steps from $\beta_t$ find its maximum. The M-step is thus itself an
iterative algorithm, as it was for the Weibull shape in @sec-weibull. The price
is specific to the logistic link: with normal errors (probit) $\ell_{\text{comp}}$
is a least-squares criterion, and the M-step is the ordinary least-squares fit
of $E(z_i \mid y_i, \beta_t)$, a truncated-normal mean, on $x_i$.

### The fixed point is the logistic MLE

At $\beta = \beta_t$, $r_i = z_i - \mu_i^{(t)} = \operatorname{logit}(U_i)$, so
$\psi(r_i) = 2U_i - 1$. Averaging over the uniform distributions of the E-step,

$$
E\big(2U_i - 1 \mid y_i, \beta_t\big) =
\begin{cases}
2\big(1 - p_i^{(t)}/2\big) - 1 = 1 - p_i^{(t)}, & y_i = 1, \\
2\big(1 - p_i^{(t)}\big)/2 - 1 = -p_i^{(t)}, & y_i = 0,
\end{cases}
\;=\; y_i - p_i^{(t)} ,
$$

and therefore

$$
\nabla_\beta Q(\beta \mid \beta_t)\Big|_{\beta = \beta_t}
= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\big(y_i - p_i^{(t)}\big) = \nabla \ell_{\text{obs}}(\beta_t),
$$

the logistic-regression score (Fisher's identity). A fixed point of EM solves
$\sum_i x_i(y_i - p_i) = 0$, which is the equation `glm` solves. Because the
integrand $2u - 1$ is linear in $u$, Gauss–Legendre quadrature computes this
gradient exactly for every $K$, so the number of nodes affects the path of the
iterates but not where they end.

### Implementation

```{r}
#| label: logit-em

### Gauss-Legendre nodes and weights on (0, 1), weights summing to 1
### (Golub-Welsch: eigen-decomposition of the Jacobi matrix)
gauss_legendre01 <- function(K) {
    j <- seq_len(K - 1); b <- j / sqrt(4 * j^2 - 1)
    J <- matrix(0, K, K); J[cbind(j, j + 1)] <- b; J[cbind(j + 1, j)] <- b
    e <- eigen(J, symmetric = TRUE)
    list(u = (rev(e$values) + 1) / 2, w = rev(e$vectors[1, ])^2)
}

### observed log-likelihood of logistic regression
loglik_logit <- function(beta, X, y) {
    eta <- drop(X %*% beta)
    sum(plogis(eta, log.p = TRUE)[y == 1]) + sum(plogis(-eta, log.p = TRUE)[y == 0])
}

### E-step: n x K matrix of pseudo-values z_ik = mu_i + logit(u_ik), with the
### nodes u_ik placed in (1 - p_i, 1) when y_i = 1 and in (0, 1 - p_i) when y_i = 0
e_step_logit <- function(beta_t, X, y, gl) {
    mu <- drop(X %*% beta_t)
    p  <- plogis(mu)
    lo <- ifelse(y == 1, 1 - p, 0)
    hi <- ifelse(y == 1, 1, 1 - p)
    mu + qlogis(lo + outer(hi - lo, gl$u))
}

### M-step: Newton's method for the logistic-error regression of the weighted
### pseudo-values on X, started at the current beta (step halving as a safeguard)
m_step_logit <- function(Z, X, w, beta, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 50) {
    Q <- function(b) sum(dlogis(Z - drop(X %*% b), log = TRUE) %*% w)
    for (it in seq_len(maxit)) {
        R    <- Z - drop(X %*% beta)
        grad <- crossprod(X, drop((2 * plogis(R) - 1) %*% w))
        hess <- crossprod(X, X * drop((2 * dlogis(R)) %*% w))   # minus the Hessian
        step <- drop(solve(hess, grad))
        Q0   <- Q(beta)
        while (Q(beta + step) < Q0 - 1e-12) step <- step / 2
        beta <- beta + step
        if (max(abs(step)) < tol) break
    }
    beta
}

em_logit <- function(X, y, beta0 = rep(0, ncol(X)), K = 20,
                     iterations = 2000, tol = 1e-9) {
    gl <- gauss_legendre01(K); beta <- beta0
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iterations + 1, ncol(X) + 1,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, c(colnames(X), "log_lik")))
    out[1, ] <- c(beta, loglik_logit(beta, X, y))
    for (i in seq_len(iterations)) {
        Z        <- e_step_logit(beta, X, y, gl)          # E-step
        beta_new <- m_step_logit(Z, X, gl$w, beta)        # M-step
        out[i + 1, ] <- c(beta_new, loglik_logit(beta_new, X, y))
        done <- max(abs(beta_new - beta)) < tol
        beta <- beta_new
        if (done) break
    }
    out[seq_len(i + 1), , drop = FALSE]
}
```

### Comparison with `glm`

Two data sets of $n = 500$ share the covariates, an intercept, a standard normal
$x_1$ and a binary $x_2$, and differ in the strength of the effects: $\beta =
(0.3, 0.5, -0.5)$ (weak) and four times that (strong). EM starts at
$\beta = 0$ and uses $K = 20$ nodes; `glm` uses its default start and a tight
convergence tolerance so that both are accurate to many digits.

```{r}
#| label: logit-data
set.seed(812)
n <- 500
X <- cbind("(Intercept)" = 1, x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5))
beta_true <- list(weak = c(0.3, 0.5, -0.5), strong = 4 * c(0.3, 0.5, -0.5))
y_logit   <- lapply(beta_true, function(b) rbinom(n, 1, plogis(drop(X %*% b))))

fits <- lapply(y_logit, function(y) {
    glm_time <- system.time(
        fit <- glm(y ~ X - 1, family = binomial, control = glm.control(epsilon = 1e-14))
    )[["elapsed"]]
    em_time <- system.time(path <- em_logit(X, y))[["elapsed"]]
    list(glm = fit, path = path, glm_time = glm_time, em_time = em_time)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-logit-compare
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| tbl-cap: "Shows that the EM algorithm built on the latent logistic variable reaches the same estimates and log-likelihood as `glm`, but needs many more iterations, especially when the effects are strong.
#|   Estimates, maximized log-likelihood, iterations and elapsed time (seconds) of `glm` and of EM ($K = 20$ quadrature nodes, started at $\\beta = 0$) on the two data sets."
cmp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(s) {
    f <- fits[[s]]; last <- f$path[nrow(f$path), ]
    data.frame(data = s, method = c("glm", "EM"),
               b0 = c(coef(f$glm)[1], last[1]), b1 = c(coef(f$glm)[2], last[2]),
               b2 = c(coef(f$glm)[3], last[3]),
               log_lik = c(as.numeric(logLik(f$glm)), last["log_lik"]),
               iterations = c(f$glm$iter, nrow(f$path) - 1),
               seconds = c(f$glm_time, f$em_time))
}))
gt::gt(cmp) |>
    gt::fmt_number(columns = c(b0, b1, b2), decimals = 6) |>
    gt::fmt_number(columns = log_lik, decimals = 6) |>
    gt::fmt_number(columns = seconds, decimals = 3) |>
    gt::cols_label(b0 = gt::md("$\\hat\\beta_0$"), b1 = gt::md("$\\hat\\beta_1$"),
                   b2 = gt::md("$\\hat\\beta_2$"), log_lik = gt::md("$\\ell_{\\text{obs}}$"))
```

The two methods agree to about six digits in every coefficient and to the
displayed precision in the log-likelihood, as the fixed-point argument
predicts. `glm` needs a handful of Newton iterations; EM needs a few times more
on the weak data set and many more on the strong one, and each EM iteration
is also more expensive (an $n \times K$ E-step and an inner Newton loop).
The next subsection explains the difference between the two data sets.

### Convergence rate and the missing information

Near the MLE $\hat\beta$, EM is the linear map
$\beta_{t+1} - \hat\beta \approx J\,(\beta_t - \hat\beta)$ with

$$
J = I - I_{\text{comp}}^{-1}\, I_{\text{obs}},
\qquad
I_{\text{obs}} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i^\top \hat p_i(1 - \hat p_i),
\qquad
I_{\text{comp}} = -\nabla^2_\beta Q(\beta \mid \hat\beta)\Big|_{\beta = \hat\beta}
= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i^\top c_i ,
$$

where $I_{\text{comp}}$ is the complete-data information given the observed
data, and $J$ is the matrix fraction of missing information. The error
eventually shrinks by the factor $\rho$, the largest eigenvalue of $J$, per
iteration. At $\beta = \hat\beta$, $f(r_i) = U_i(1 - U_i)$, so
$c_i = E\{2U_i(1 - U_i) \mid y_i\}$ with $U_i$ uniform on $(a_i, b_i)$:

$$
c_i = \frac{2\{G(b_i) - G(a_i)\}}{b_i - a_i},
\qquad G(u) = \frac{u^2}{2} - \frac{u^3}{3} .
$$

When $\hat p_i = 1/2$, $c_i = 1/3$ while $\hat p_i(1 - \hat p_i) = 1/4$, so a
unit carries $3/4$ of its complete-data information and the missing fraction
is $1/4$. When $\hat p_i$ is near 0 or 1, $\hat p_i(1 - \hat p_i) \to 0$ while
$c_i$ for the likely outcome stays near $1/3$: knowing that $z_i$ landed on the
side of 0 where it almost surely lands says almost nothing about where $z_i$
is, so nearly all the information about $z_i$ is missing. Strong effects push
many $\hat p_i$ toward 0 and 1, $\rho$ toward 1, and EM slows down.

```{r}
#| label: logit-rate
em_rate_logit <- function(beta, X, y) {
    p  <- plogis(drop(X %*% beta))
    lo <- ifelse(y == 1, 1 - p, 0); hi <- ifelse(y == 1, 1, 1 - p)
    G  <- function(u) u^2 / 2 - u^3 / 3
    I_comp <- crossprod(X, X * 2 * (G(hi) - G(lo)) / (hi - lo))
    I_obs  <- crossprod(X, X * p * (1 - p))
    max(Mod(eigen(diag(ncol(X)) - solve(I_comp, I_obs), only.values = TRUE)$values))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-logit-paths
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates that the convergence rate of EM for logistic regression is set by the fraction of missing information, which is larger when the effects are strong.
#|   Distance $\\|\\beta_t - \\hat\\beta\\|$ of the EM iterates from the MLE (log scale) on the two data sets; the dashed lines have the slopes $\\log_{10}\\rho$ predicted by the largest eigenvalue $\\rho$ of $I - I_{\\text{comp}}^{-1} I_{\\text{obs}}$."
cols <- c(weak = "steelblue", strong = "firebrick")
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, max(sapply(fits, function(f) nrow(f$path)))),
     ylim = c(-10, 1), xlab = "EM iteration t",
     ylab = expression(log[10] * " ||" * beta[t] - hat(beta) * "||"))
rho <- sapply(names(fits), function(s) {
    f <- fits[[s]]; bhat <- coef(f$glm)
    err <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(f$path[, 1:3, drop = FALSE], 2, bhat)^2))
    t <- seq_along(err) - 1
    lines(t, log10(err), type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = cols[s])
    r <- em_rate_logit(bhat, X, y_logit[[s]])
```
